claim: Cold temperature is prevalent across the biosphere and slows the rates of chemical reactions.
source: Cold temperature is prevalent across the biosphere and slows the rates of chemical reactions.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the effect of temperature on reaction rates, supported by citations in the text (Arrhenius, 1889; Wolfenden et al., 1999).

claim: Increased catalysis has been predicted to be a dominant adaptive trait of enzymes to reduced temperature.
source: Increased catalysis has been predicted to be a dominant adaptive trait of enzymes to reduced temperature, and this expectation has informed physical models for enzyme catalysis and influenced bioprospecting strategies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and represents a prevailing hypothesis in the field.

claim: The expectation of increased catalysis in cold adaptation has informed physical models for enzyme catalysis.
source: Increased catalysis has been predicted to be a dominant adaptive trait of enzymes to reduced temperature, and this expectation has informed physical models for enzyme catalysis and influenced bioprospecting strategies.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the rate compensation model and is supported by citations to physical models (Feller and Gerday, 2003; Fields et al., 2015; Åqvist et al., 2017; Arcus et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2017; Saavedra et al., 2018).

claim: The expectation of increased catalysis in cold adaptation has influenced bioprospecting strategies.
source: Increased catalysis has been predicted to be a dominant adaptive trait of enzymes to reduced temperature, and this expectation has informed physical models for enzyme catalysis and influenced bioprospecting strategies.
evidence: This is supported by citations to bioprospecting literature (Bhatia et al., 2021; Bruno et al., 2019; Kuddus, 2018; Santiago et al., 2016).

claim: 2223 enzyme reactions were paired with their organism's optimal growth temperature for analysis.
source: To systematically test rate enhancement as an adaptive trait to cold, we paired kinetic constants of 2223 enzyme reactions with their organism's optimal growth temperature (TGrowth) and analyzed trends of rate constants as a function of TGrowth.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental approach and dataset size used in the study.

claim: The data do not support a general increase in rate enhancement in cold adaptation.
source: These data do not support a general increase in rate enhancement in cold adaptation.
evidence: This is the primary conclusion from the analysis of 2223 enzyme reactions, supported by the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: In ketosteroid isomerase (KSI), there is prior evidence for temperature adaptation from a change in an active site residue that results in a tradeoff between activity and stability.
source: In the model enzyme ketosteroid isomerase (KSI), there is prior evidence for temperature adaptation from a change in an active site residue that results in a tradeoff between activity and stability.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Pinney et al., 2021).

claim: Little of the rate constant variation for 20 KSI variants was accounted for by TGrowth.
source: Nevertheless, we found that little of the rate constant variation for 20 KSI variants was accounted for by TGrowth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on 20 KSI variants presented in Figure 3.

claim: A correlation between stability and TGrowth was observed across 433 proteins.
source: In contrast, and consistent with prior expectations, we observed a correlation between stability and TGrowth across 433 proteins.
evidence: This is supported by data from ProThermDB presented in Figure 4.

claim: Temperature exerts a weaker selection pressure on enzyme rate constants than stability.
source: These results suggest that temperature exerts a weaker selection pressure on enzyme rate constants than stability and that evolutionary forces other than temperature are responsible for the majority of enzymatic rate constant variation.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of rate and stability data across the study.

claim: Evolutionary forces other than temperature are responsible for the majority of enzymatic rate constant variation.
source: These results suggest that temperature exerts a weaker selection pressure on enzyme rate constants than stability and that evolutionary forces other than temperature are responsible for the majority of enzymatic rate constant variation.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between rate constants and TGrowth.

claim: The maintenance of enzyme rates has been suggested to be a universal challenge for organisms at colder temperatures that do not regulate their internal temperature.
source: As reaction rates are reduced at lower temperatures (Arrhenius, 1889; Wolfenden et al., 1999), the maintenance of enzyme rates has been suggested to be a universal challenge for organisms at colder temperatures that do not regulate their internal temperature (D'Amico et al., 2003; Fields et al., 2015; Siddiqui and Cavicchioli, 2006; Zecchinon et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: According to the rate compensation model, cold-adapted enzyme variants provide more rate enhancement than warm-adapted variants.
source: According to what we term the rate compensation model of temperature adaptation, this challenge has been suggested to be met by cold-adapted enzyme variants providing more rate enhancement than the corresponding warm-adapted variants (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the rate compensation model, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The rate compensation model predicts that cold-adapted variants are generally faster than warm-adapted variants when assayed at a common temperature.
source: This model predicts that cold-adapted variants are generally faster than warm-adapted variants when assayed at a common temperature (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a prediction of the rate compensation model, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Rate compensation behavior has been reported for diverse enzymes.
source: Indeed, this behavior has been reported for diverse enzymes, and these observations have been taken as support for this model (Figure 1C and D; Collins and Gerday, 2017; Feller and Gerday, 1997; Siddiqui and Cavicchioli, 2006; Smalås et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: The observed effects on enzymatic rate constants have led to proposals of general physical models for cold adaptation linked to flexibility.
source: The observed effects on enzymatic rate constants (Figure 1C and D) have also led to proposals of general physical models for cold adaptation linked to flexibility, as outlined in Feller and Gerday, 2003; Fields et al., 2015; Åqvist et al., 2017; Arcus et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2017; Saavedra et al., 2018.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to physical models.

claim: Features identified in comparative structural analyses of cold- and warm-adapted enzymes include fewer surface hydrogen bonds and salt bridges.
source: Further, features identified in comparative structural analyses of cold- and warm-adapted enzymes, such as fewer surface hydrogen bonds and salt bridges (Cai et al., 2018), have been suggested to increase flexibility and thereby increase catalysis (Mandelman et al., 2019; Park et al., 2018a; Park et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Fewer surface hydrogen bonds and salt bridges have been suggested to increase flexibility and thereby increase catalysis.
source: Further, features identified in comparative structural analyses of cold- and warm-adapted enzymes, such as fewer surface hydrogen bonds and salt bridges (Cai et al., 2018), have been suggested to increase flexibility and thereby increase catalysis (Mandelman et al., 2019; Park et al., 2018a; Park et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The study of cold adaptation may have the potential to provide generalizable insights into physical properties of enzymes that make them better catalysts.
source: Correspondingly, the study of cold adaptation may have the potential to provide generalizable insights into physical properties of enzymes that make them better catalysts, a longstanding challenge in the field (Blow, 2000; Hammes et al., 2011; Kraut et al., 2003; Ringe and Petsko, 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential implications of cold adaptation studies, supported by citations to the challenge of understanding enzyme catalysis.

claim: The prediction of enhanced catalysis by cold-adapted enzymes has motivated low-temperature bioprospecting for biocatalysts to use in industrial processes.
source: From a practical perspective, the prediction of enhanced catalysis by cold-adapted enzymes has motivated low-temperature bioprospecting for biocatalysts to use in industrial processes (Bhatia et al., 2021; Bruno et al., 2019; Kuddus, 2018; Santiago et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to bioprospecting literature.

claim: Of 76,083 kcat values in BRENDA, 49,314 were for wild-type enzymes.
source: Of 76,083 kcat values in BRENDA, we found that 49,314 were for wild-type enzymes.
evidence: This is a direct statement of data filtering from the BRENDA database.

claim: 16,543 kcat values matched to microorganisms with known TGrowth values.
source: Of these data, 16,543 values matched to microorganisms with known TGrowth values.
evidence: This is a direct statement of data matching results.

claim: 7086 kcat values for 2223 reactions across 815 organisms with at least two variants per reaction were selected.
source: We selected reactions in the database with variants from more than one organism, spanning 7086 kcat values for 2223 reactions across 815 organisms with at least two variants per reaction (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the dataset used for analysis, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The reactions spanned a temperature range of 1–83°C.
source: These reactions spanned a temperature range of 1–83°C (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the temperature range in the dataset, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 1142 reactions had rate ratios greater than one.
source: We observed rate ratios greater than one (1142 reactions) as predicted by rate compensation, but nearly the same number of rate ratios of less than one (1082 reactions) (Figure 2C, compare with Figure 1D), providing no support for widespread or predominant rate compensation.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data analysis results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 1082 reactions had rate ratios of less than one.
source: We observed rate ratios greater than one (1142 reactions) as predicted by rate compensation, but nearly the same number of rate ratios of less than one (1082 reactions) (Figure 2C, compare with Figure 1D), providing no support for widespread or predominant rate compensation.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data analysis results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 615 reactions had more than one variant assigned the same TGrowth.
source: We found 615 reactions with more than one variant assigned the same TGrowth, and we calculated the rate ratio and its reciprocal (kmax/kmin and kmin/kmax) for each reaction.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the control dataset used for comparison.

claim: The control distribution was indistinguishable from the data distribution of rate ratios across TGrowth.
source: This control distribution (dashed line, Figure 2D) was indistinguishable from the data distribution of rate ratios across TGrowth (solid line, Figure 2D; p = 0.21, Mann–Whitney U test, two-sided).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney U test) and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Two reactions (triose-phosphate isomerase with glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate and cutinase with 4-nitrophenyl butyrate) were significantly but positively associated with TGrowth.
source: We found two reactions (triose-phosphate isomerase with glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate and cutinase with 4-nitrophenyl butyrate) significantly but positively associated with TGrowth (Bonferroni correction; p-value < 5.3 × 10–5, n = 951).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis with Bonferroni correction and shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: The change of a single active site residue at position 103 from serine to protonated aspartic acid in KSI provided improved activity from a stronger hydrogen bond while also sacrificing stability.
source: Specifically, the change of a single active site residue at position 103 from serine (S103, prevalently found in warm-adapted KSI variants) to protonated aspartic acid (D103, prevalently found in mesophilic KSI variants) provided improved activity from a stronger hydrogen bond while also sacrificing stability by introducing an unfavorable protonation coupled to folding.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Pinney et al., 2021).

claim: 20 KSI variants were assayed that vary in sequence and TGrowth.
source: We therefore used KSI to more deeply investigate the potential for rate compensation by assaying 20 variants that vary in sequence and TGrowth (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental approach, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The 20 selected KSI variants ranged between 20% and 75% sequence identity to each other.
source: The 20 selected KSI variants ranged between 20% and 75% sequence identity to each other (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and were selected from bacteria originating from environments spanning glaciers, ocean floor, soil, and wastewater with reported TGrowth values from 15°C to 46°C (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the sequence diversity in the KSI variants, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: KSI variants were selected from bacteria with reported TGrowth values from 15°C to 46°C.
source: The 20 selected KSI variants ranged between 20% and 75% sequence identity to each other (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and were selected from bacteria originating from environments spanning glaciers, ocean floor, soil, and wastewater with reported TGrowth values from 15°C to 46°C (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the temperature range of the organisms from which KSI variants were selected.

claim: Each purified KSI demonstrated similar circular dichroism (CD) spectra at 5°C and 25°C.
source: Each purified KSI demonstrated similar circular dichroism (CD) spectra at 5°C and 25°C, suggesting that variants were not unfolding at the 25°C assay temperature (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: All putative KSI variants exhibited isomerase activity on the steroid substrate 5 (10)-estrene-3,17-dione (5 (10)-EST).
source: All putative KSI variants exhibited isomerase activity on the steroid substrate 5 (10)-estrene-3,17-dione (5 (10)-EST) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental activity measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The KSIs with the prevalent cold-adapted residue (D103 and E103) were not uniformly faster than other KSIs in kcat.
source: We observed that the KSIs with the prevalent cold-adapted residue (D103 and the similar residue E103, Pseudomonas putida numbering) were not uniformly faster than other KSIs in kcat (Figure 3C) or kcat/KM (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: One of the fastest KSI variants contained serine at position 103.
source: The observation that one of the fastest variants contained serine at this position indicates that there are additional factors that influence its rate enhancement (Figure 3C and see Discussion).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: For KSI, the value of kcat decreased as a function of TGrowth with a shallow slope (mrate = –0.006, p = 0.02).
source: For KSI, the value of kcat decreased as a function of TGrowth, but the shallow slope (mrate = –0.006, p = 0.02) (Figure 3D) and the small coefficient of determination (R2 = 0.01) of this relationship indicate that TGrowth accounts for little of the observed 80-fold rate variation.
evidence: This is supported by linear regression analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: TGrowth accounts for little of the observed 80-fold rate variation in KSI.
source: For KSI, the value of kcat decreased as a function of TGrowth, but the shallow slope (mrate = –0.006, p = 0.02) (Figure 3D) and the small coefficient of determination (R2 = 0.01) of this relationship indicate that TGrowth accounts for little of the observed 80-fold rate variation.
evidence: This is inferred from the low R2 value (0.01) of the linear regression shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The mean temperature optimum of enzymes correlates well with organism TGrowth (r = 0.75).
source: Prior work has shown that the mean temperature optimum of enzymes correlates well with organism TGrowth (r = 0.75, Engqvist, 2018), but enzyme temperature optima reflect a combination of rate and stability effects.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Engqvist, 2018).

claim: Enzyme temperature optima reflect a combination of rate and stability effects.
source: Prior work has shown that the mean temperature optimum of enzymes correlates well with organism TGrowth (r = 0.75, Engqvist, 2018), but enzyme temperature optima reflect a combination of rate and stability effects.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the interpretation of temperature optima.

claim: Across 433 wild-type variants in ProThermDB, a significant relationship between Tm and TGrowth was observed (R2 = 0.43, p = 2 × 10–54).
source: Across 433 wild-type variants present in this database, we observed a significant relationship between Tm and TGrowth (Figure 4A, R2 = 0.43, p = 2 × 10–54).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data from ProThermDB shown in Figure 4A.

claim: For the 43 protein families with more than one reported variant, 39 had a higher melting temperature than their cold-adapted counterpart.
source: For the 43 protein families with more than one reported variant, 39 had a higher melting temperature than their cold-adapted counterpart (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by data from ProThermDB shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Cold-adapted enzyme variants are not generally faster than their warm-adapted counterparts.
source: Our results do not support this intuitive and common model as we found that cold-adapted enzyme variants are not generally faster than their warm-adapted counterparts.
evidence: This is the primary conclusion from the analysis of 2223 enzyme reactions.

claim: Stability is the dominant driving force underlying the previously identified changes in KSI.
source: Even though there was prior evidence for temperature adaptation of the enzyme KSI that is accompanied by rate effects, we found that little of its overall rate variation was accounted for by organismal TGrowth, suggesting instead that stability is the dominant driving force underlying the previously identified changes.
evidence: This is inferred from the low correlation between KSI rate and TGrowth combined with the known stability effects.

claim: Enzyme rate enhancement is unlikely to be the primary trait selected for during adaptation to colder environmental temperatures.
source: Our observations suggest that enzyme rate enhancement is unlikely to be the primary trait selected for during adaptation to colder environmental temperatures, broadly and in the model system KSI.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between rate and TGrowth across multiple datasets.

claim: Most enzymes operate well below the diffusional limit.
source: However, most enzymes operate well below the diffusional limit (Bar-Even et al., 2011), underscoring that an optimal reaction rate constant may be different than the maximal enzyme rate constant.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Bar-Even et al., 2011).

claim: An optimal reaction rate constant may be different than the maximal enzyme rate constant.
source: However, most enzymes operate well below the diffusional limit (Bar-Even et al., 2011), underscoring that an optimal reaction rate constant may be different than the maximal enzyme rate constant.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that most enzymes operate below the diffusional limit.

claim: Rate optimization in vivo may be accomplished by altering gene expression.
source: Rate optimization in vivo may be accomplished by altering gene expression (Somero, 2004), isoform expression (Somero, 1995), or cellular pH and osmolytes (Hochachka and Lewis, 1971; Yancey and Somero, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Rate optimization in vivo may be accomplished by altering isoform expression.
source: Rate optimization in vivo may be accomplished by altering gene expression (Somero, 2004), isoform expression (Somero, 1995), or cellular pH and osmolytes (Hochachka and Lewis, 1971; Yancey and Somero, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Rate optimization in vivo may be accomplished by altering cellular pH and osmolytes.
source: Rate optimization in vivo may be accomplished by altering gene expression (Somero, 2004), isoform expression (Somero, 1995), or cellular pH and osmolytes (Hochachka and Lewis, 1971; Yancey and Somero, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The optimal enzyme rate may be lower than the maximal rate to channel metabolites and coordinate metabolism.
source: Alternatively, the optimal enzyme rate may be lower than the maximal rate to channel metabolites and coordinate metabolism (Prentice et al., 2020; Wortel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Models of enzyme-metabolite pathway evolution predict that the subset of enzymes that govern pathway flux through rate-limiting steps are under strong rate selection.
source: Further, models of enzyme-metabolite pathway evolution predict that the subset of enzymes that govern pathway flux through rate-limiting steps are under strong rate selection (Noda-Garcia et al., 2018), and it is also possible that maximal enzyme rates are not evolutionarily accessible (Obolski et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Noda-Garcia et al., 2018).

claim: Maximal enzyme rates may not be evolutionarily accessible.
source: Further, models of enzyme-metabolite pathway evolution predict that the subset of enzymes that govern pathway flux through rate-limiting steps are under strong rate selection (Noda-Garcia et al., 2018), and it is also possible that maximal enzyme rates are not evolutionarily accessible (Obolski et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Obolski et al., 2018).

claim: Rate compensation may be more probable for highly related species that live in similar environments.
source: We speculate that rate compensation may be more probable for highly related species that live in similar environments, such as marine species that live at different latitudes or depths but otherwise experience little environmental difference (Dong and Somero, 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about when rate compensation might occur, supported by citation to an example (Dong and Somero, 2009).

claim: The temperature dependence of protein unfolding may exert a larger driving force on adaptation than the temperature dependence of rate.
source: The temperature dependence of protein unfolding (Becktel and Schellman, 1987) may exert a larger driving force on adaptation than the temperature dependence of rate.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed correlation between stability and TGrowth but not rate and TGrowth, supported by citation to the temperature dependence of unfolding.

claim: Misfolded protein has been demonstrated to have deleterious fitness effects.
source: There may be an additional strong selection pressure to avoid unfolded states, as misfolded protein has been demonstrated to have deleterious fitness effects (Geiler-Samerotte et al., 2011) and cells expend considerable energy to clear misfolded variants using chaperones and degradation pathways (Clague and Urbé, 2010; Hartl et al., 2011; Lund, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Geiler-Samerotte et al., 2011).

claim: Cells expend considerable energy to clear misfolded variants using chaperones and degradation pathways.
source: There may be an additional strong selection pressure to avoid unfolded states, as misfolded protein has been demonstrated to have deleterious fitness effects (Geiler-Samerotte et al., 2011) and cells expend considerable energy to clear misfolded variants using chaperones and degradation pathways (Clague and Urbé, 2010; Hartl et al., 2011; Lund, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Adaptive paths toward stability may be more abundant and more accessible than analogous paths toward rate enhancement.
source: Additionally, adaptive paths toward stability may be more abundant and more accessible than analogous paths toward rate enhancement, given that each protein may be stabilized individually through a wide variety of mechanisms (Hart et al., 2014) and less constrained by biological context than an enzyme evolving synergistically with complex metabolic networks.
evidence: This is a speculative statement inferred from the variety of stabilization mechanisms and the complexity of metabolic networks, supported by citation (Hart et al., 2014).

claim: Each protein may be stabilized individually through a wide variety of mechanisms.
source: Additionally, adaptive paths toward stability may be more abundant and more accessible than analogous paths toward rate enhancement, given that each protein may be stabilized individually through a wide variety of mechanisms (Hart et al., 2014) and less constrained by biological context than an enzyme evolving synergistically with complex metabolic networks.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Hart et al., 2014).

claim: 158,184 positions from 1005 enzyme families vary with growth temperature.
source: The recent discovery of 158,184 positions from 1005 enzyme families that vary with growth temperature may further expand our understanding of the molecular strategies that underlie protein stabilization (Pinney et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Pinney et al., 2021).

claim: The observation that KSI variants from high temperature correlate with serine at position 103 may reflect selection for the stabilizing effects of S103.
source: The observation that KSI variants from high temperature correlate with serine at position 103 may reflect selection for the stabilizing effects of S103 (Pinney et al., 2021).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation and supported by citation to prior work (Pinney et al., 2021).

claim: The msKSI variant with the wild-type serine residue mutated to aspartic acid (S103D) has increased activity and decreased stability.
source: As observed with other KSI variants, the msKSI variant with the wild-type serine residue mutated to aspartic acid (S103D) has increased activity and decreased stability.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Pinney et al., 2021).

claim: In msKSI, the decreased stability from the S103D mutation renders it partially unfolded even in the absence of denaturants.
source: However, in msKSI, the decreased stability from the S103D mutation renders it partially unfolded even in the absence of denaturants (Pinney et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Pinney et al., 2021).

claim: Drift or other factors may have led to an overall destabilized scaffold in msKSI.
source: This result suggests a model where drift or other factors have led to an overall destabilized scaffold, such that msKSI cannot accommodate the activating S103D change (without unfolding) and has made other as yet unidentified amino acid changes to increase activity.
evidence: This is a speculative model inferred from the observation that msKSI cannot accommodate the S103D mutation.

claim: Flexibility has been posited to mechanistically link rate and stability.
source: Flexibility has been posited to mechanistically link rate and stability, with multiple underlying interconnections discussed (see Supplementary file 1; Åqvist et al., 2017; Arcus et al., 2016; D'Amico et al., 2003; Daniel and Danson, 2010; Nguyen et al., 2017; Saavedra et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Most motions in an enzyme are not expected to be coupled to the enzyme reaction coordinate.
source: Nevertheless, there are many degrees of freedom in an enzyme and most motions are not expected to be coupled to the enzyme reaction coordinate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about enzyme dynamics.

claim: The absence of widespread rate compensation to temperature in contrast to observed stability compensation is consistent with the perspective that most motions are not coupled to the reaction coordinate.
source: Our observation of the absence of widespread rate compensation to temperature in contrast to observed stability compensation is consistent with this perspective, as are prior examples of enzyme stabilization in the absence of detrimental rate effects (Minges et al., 2019; Miyazaki et al., 2000; Siddiqui, 2017; Wintrode and Arnold, 2000; Zhao and Feng, 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citations to prior examples.

claim: Prior examples exist of enzyme stabilization in the absence of detrimental rate effects.
source: Our observation of the absence of widespread rate compensation to temperature in contrast to observed stability compensation is consistent with this perspective, as are prior examples of enzyme stabilization in the absence of detrimental rate effects (Minges et al., 2019; Miyazaki et al., 2000; Siddiqui, 2017; Wintrode and Arnold, 2000; Zhao and Feng, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: KSI catalyzes the double bond isomerization of steroid substrates.
source: KSI catalyzes the double bond isomerization of steroid substrates (Figure 3B) and is predicted to be part of a pathway that enables degradation of steroids for energy and carbon metabolism in bacteria (Horinouchi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about KSI function, illustrated in Figure 3B and supported by citation.

claim: KSI is predicted to be part of a pathway that enables degradation of steroids for energy and carbon metabolism in bacteria.
source: KSI catalyzes the double bond isomerization of steroid substrates (Figure 3B) and is predicted to be part of a pathway that enables degradation of steroids for energy and carbon metabolism in bacteria (Horinouchi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Horinouchi et al., 2010).

claim: The median rate ratio (kcold/kwarm) for 2223 reactions is 1.1-fold with 95% CI [1.00, 1.22].
source: (C) Rate ratio distribution of the rate at the coldest TGrowth (kcold) divided by the rate of the variant from the warmest TGrowth (kwarm) (median = 1.1-fold, 95% CI [1.00, 1.22], n = 2223 reactions).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the statistical summary of the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The median rate ratio for the control distribution (same TGrowth) is 1.0-fold with 95% CI [0.89, 1.13] for 615 reactions.
source: (D) Rate ratio (kcold/kwarm) data (solid line, n = 2223 from panel C) compared to fold change control distribution (same TGrowth; dashed line, median = 1.0-fold, 95% CI [0.89, 1.13], n = 615 reactions; p = 0.21, Mann–Whitney U test, two-sided).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the statistical summary of the control data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The median kcat/KM rate ratio (kcold/kwarm) is 0.93-fold with 95% CI [0.78, 1.12] for 953 reactions.
source: (C) kcat/KM rate ratio (kcold/kwarm) distribution (median = 0.93-fold, 95% CI [0.78, 1.12], n = 953 reactions).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the statistical summary of the kcat/KM data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The median kcat/KM rate ratio for the control is 1.00-fold with 95% CI [0.82, 1.21] for 307 reactions.
source: (D) kcat/KM rate ratio (kcold/kwarm) data (black line, n = 953 reactions) with kcat/KM rate ratio control (gray line, median = 1.00-fold, 95% CI [0.82, 1.21], n = 307 reactions) determined in the same way as the kcat rate ratio control in the main text (see Materials and methods) (p = 0.80, Mann–Whitney U test, two-sided).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the statistical summary of the kcat/KM control data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The median fold change (Tm cold/Tm warm) for 43 protein families is 0.81 with 95% CI [0.70, 0.85].
source: (B) Fold change (Tm cold/Tm warm) of wild-type protein variants (n = 43, median = 0.81, 95% [0.70, 0.85]).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the statistical summary of the stability data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 5 (10)-EST was used to allow direct measurement of the rate-limiting chemical step kcat.
source: 5 (10)-EST was used to allow direct measurement of the rate-limiting chemical step kcat (Pollack et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Pollack et al., 1986) and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The prior conclusion of widespread temperature adaptation may have arisen from the use of a small set of enzymes (n = 28).
source: The prior conclusion of widespread temperature adaptation may have arisen from the use of a small set of enzymes (n = 28; Figure 1C and D) or from inadvertent confirmation bias (Nickerson, 1998).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of the small prior dataset (Figure 1C and D) with the larger current dataset.

claim: The prior conclusion of widespread temperature adaptation may have arisen from inadvertent confirmation bias.
source: The prior conclusion of widespread temperature adaptation may have arisen from the use of a small set of enzymes (n = 28; Figure 1C and D) or from inadvertent confirmation bias (Nickerson, 1998).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the discrepancy between prior conclusions and current findings, supported by citation to confirmation bias (Nickerson, 1998).
